title: Banks propose regional hubs to kill levy threat
full_text:
Australia's top banks want to work together to run financial service hubs in the bush under a proposed new industry model to address their declining physical presence and avoid a costly intervention from Canberra.
Under a plan hatched by the Australian Banking Association, participating lenders would each chip in to bring face-to-face banking and cash services hubs to up to 10 towns currently without a branch, with a view to rolling out more if successful.
The hubs would either be opened in Australia Post outlets, council offices and libraries, or operate out of modular "bank in a box" units, run by the ABA and funded by the banks.
They would include multi-bank ATMs and concierge staff who would be restricted from providing advice or facilitating transactions under current regulatory settings.
The ABA is asking the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission for an almost three-year authorisation, so its members - which include the big four banks, Macquarie, ING, Bank of Queensland and others - can iron out the final details.
"This is an industry-led package that will ensure regional customers have continued access to face-to-face banking services," ABA chief executive Simon Birmingham said.
Its application to the ACCC, viewed by The Australian Financial Review, also proposes developing industry-wide commitments to keeping regional services running, especially in remote, sparsely populated or vulnerable areas that aren't otherwise commercially viable.
Regional branch numbers have declined by 38 per cent since 2017, according to APRA data. If ACCC authorisation is granted, it would be up to each bank to decide the extent to which they participate, with the proposed location of the 10 hubs remaining confidential.
The ABA's application claimed an industry solution had Treasury support and that without it, the banks risked a "regulatory intervention that may be less efficient or less responsive to the needs of regional communities".
Treasurer Jim Chalmers first proposed a regional banking levy in 2024 in response to a public backlash against branch closures. Such a measure would force some banks to cough up tens of millions of dollars to directly support regional competitors.
The threat encouraged some lenders to pursue alternative solutions, including an ACCC-approved ABA-led trial to roll out 20 ATMs across regional areas.
Commonwealth Bank has committed to investing $140 million to upgrade its branch network after Westpac began rotating bankers through regional areas to address service gaps.
Last week, CBA matched Westpac in extending its moratorium on regional bank closures until 2030, while ANZ and National Australia Bank's own commitments are due to expire halfway through next year.
These branches remain a cost burden for the big four and the ABA said there was no guarantee that further moratoriums would be agreed to.
ANZ's integration of Suncorp is expected to conclude at the same time as its moratorium next year, with the bank expected to assess duplication across its branch network as part of its simplification strategy.
The Regional Banking Investment Alliance, representing 24 small institutions, has separately advocated for a different model that would force the nine largest banks to cross-subsidise regional competitors to the tune of $153 million a year.
Regional Australia Bank chief executive David Heine, a member of the RBIA, said last week that the levy remained a live option.
"We're optimistic that our proposal will be well received by both the bureaucrats and the politicians within Canberra, and we absolutely know that it will be well received by the regional Australian voting public," he said.
Heine expressed doubt that the ABA would be able to align the sector around a single long-term solution for banking in the bush.
"This is an issue where there are presently winners and losers and as a consequence, I think it's impractical to think that we can, as a total industry, galvanise around a single solution," he said.
"I suspect that the ABA is having a very difficult time finding a single line through this complex challenge," Heine said.
